analysis.one_liner: Makes the Bush-era income tax cuts permanent and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: A single House Republican introduced the bill with no cosponsors; it died in committee without a hearing or vote as Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made all of the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent instead of expiring, including lower income tax rates at the top and the 15% rate on investment income, and would have permanently repealed the estate tax, which falls only on estates over roughly $5 million. It also permanently raised the exemption for the alternative minimum tax, which mainly protects middle- and upper-middle-income households, and let certain tax credits apply against that tax. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and received no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthiest households and large estates gain most: the top income tax rates, the 15% capital gains and dividend rates, and full estate tax repeal would all be locked in. Middle-income families with children gain from the expanded child tax credit and AMT relief.

how_it_helps.text: Makes permanent all provisions of the 2001 tax cut law, including the top-rate and other rate reductions that were scheduled to expire after 2010.
Makes permanent the reduced 15% tax rates on capital gains and dividends from the 2003 law.
Permanently repeals the federal estate tax, which applies only to very large inheritances.
Permanently increases the alternative minimum tax exemption amount annually from 2010 to 2020 and allows certain nonrefundable credits, such as the child tax credit, to offset the AMT.
Repeals Title IX of the 2001 law, the sunset provisions that would have ended all of those tax cuts after 2010.

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury: forgoing these revenues increases deficits and debt, shifting the eventual cost to future taxpayers. Estates over the exemption threshold lose nothing to the tax, while revenue that funds public services is permanently reduced.

drawbacks.text: Permanently repealing the estate tax eliminates the only federal tax on very large inheritances, a benefit concentrated among the top estates.
Locking in the rate cuts and estate repeal permanently forgoes revenue indefinitely, increasing deficits rather than allowing the scheduled expiration to restore balance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The AMT fix addresses a real middle-class problem, but it is paired with permanent extension of tax cuts whose largest benefits flow to high earners and a full estate tax repeal that benefits a very small number of the largest estates; the revenue cost is the tradeoff.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Connie Mack introduced the bill on December 16, 2010, during the lame-duck session of the 111th Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced.
No further legislative action occurred; the bill had no cosponsors and died at the end of the Congress.
The bill was introduced the same week Congress was negotiating the bipartisan compromise that extended the 2001/2003 tax cuts for two years rather than permanently.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained directly, because the bill never became law; the concentrated beneficiaries of the tax cuts it would have made permanent gained nothing from this vehicle, and the estate tax remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Estate tax stayed; no one gained

for.name: Rep. Connie Mack
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means; the bill's only sponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action, allowing the bill to die without a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors, and no votes or floor action, so no partisan division was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently repealed the estate tax on very large inheritances, a benefit limited to a small number of the wealthiest families.

industries.industry: High earners and investment income holders
industries.note: Permanent extension of the top tax rates and the 15% capital gains and dividend rates delivers the largest dollar benefits to the highest incomes.
The bill would have permanently fixed the AMT and preserved the child tax credit, providing real middle-class tax relief, though these gains are paired with large revenue losses.
